title: King's Indian: model games
outcomes: Predicts the next move at thirteen decision points in three real King's Indian games between players rated above 2,500, and names what decided each game with the engine's numbers
Says in a sentence what each side is doing in the Classical line with Ne1 (White's c5 break against Black's f4, g5 and g4 advance) and in the line with b4 and Ng5
Names the capture that cost a game in each of two games (the knight taking on b4, the queen taking on c4) and finds the safer move
Reads our master counts at the branch point and says what they do and do not show
Teaches the three games back in a few sentences, with one typical mistake for each side
sources: library/data/games (TWIC weekly zips and Lichess broadcast PGN, 2012 to 2026): games starting 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6 with both players rated 2500 or more were collected by script (3,855 games) and engines excluded by name; three games chosen by hand, their moves and results read with python-chess. Game A: Kasimdzhanov - Nakamura, 1st FIDE Grand Prix, London, 22 Sep 2012, 0-1 (2684 and 2783). Game B: So - Ding Liren, 8th Grand Slam Masters, Bilbao, 26 Oct 2015, 1-0 (2760 and 2782). Game C: Wang Hao - Bacrot, 45th Biel GM, 23 Jul 2012, 1-0 (2739 and 2713). Moves and results are facts; every comment is our own wording [S]

app/public/masters/stats.json (329,379 games, both players 2500+, first 24 plies, built 2026-10-29): after 8...Ne7 the listed continuations sum to 613 games (b4 307 games, White won 136, drew 107, lost 64; Ne1 198 games, 81/74/43); after b4: Nh5 138 games 58/53/27, a5 122 games 52/39/31, Ne8 38 games 22/11/5; after Ne1: Nd7 140 games 58/42/40, Ne8 44 games 22/20/2; the data include engine games from broadcasts [V]
Engine claims: Stockfish 19 lite, single thread, depth 16, in content/items/lesson-od-l-od-kid-7.json and the board claims of this lesson; evidence under recorded limits, not proof [V]
Purposes of moves on game boards are the usual textbook ideas and are stated as aims, not verified outcomes [R]; conjecture is labelled [H] or [I] in the text

steps.text: **Two plans, one race.** White opens the queenside, Black the kingside. Whoever lands the first real blow gains time; a blow that loses material is not a blow. In our masters tree (329,379 games, both players 2500+; it includes engine games) the position after the knight move to e7 occurs 613 times. White chose the b-pawn push in 307 games (won 136, drew 107, lost 64) and the knight retreat in 198 (81, 74, 43). Both are played; the counts show popularity, not truth. [V]

steps.text: **What decided game C.** Black's attack was working: the engine had Black ahead until the queen took the pawn on c4 [V, depth 16]. [I] A good attack can be thrown away by a greedy capture: ask what the capture does to the piece that was making the threats. In games B and C one capture did. [H] In these three games the plan got a position and one move decided it.

**What the games share.** Each side had a plan: a queenside break and knight play, a pawn storm. In game A White lost the e6 pawn, then slipped with the king. In game B Black's extra sacrifice failed. In game C Black's attack worked until a greedy capture. Masters tree, after the b-pawn push: Black played the knight to h5 in 138 games (White won 58, drew 53, lost 27) and the a-pawn push in 122 (52, 39, 31). Small samples: popularity, not best play. [V]

steps.prompt: Pick one of the three games. Name the move that decided it and the move that should have been played, in your own words.

steps.text:
**Recap.**
- [I] Opposite wings, so speed counts.
- A pawn move gains time when it attacks something. [V]
- A capture is free only if you count the defenders and the follow-up. [V]
- Game A: White lost the e6 pawn, then slipped with the king. Game B: one capture. Game C: Black's attack worked until one capture. [V]
- [I] The plan gets you a position; the next move decides.
- Counts show popularity, not truth.
